problem: Existing zero-shot GPT-based VLN agents (NavGPT, DiscussNav) decide only among locally adjacent navigable points, with no global view of the environment. Once they go wrong they wander aimlessly instead of backtracking deliberately. They also rely on multi-expert, text-only pipelines that convert vision to captions (losing information), cost many tokens, cannot directly use multimodal GPT-4V, and were validated only on R2R step-by-step instructions.
motivation: LLM agents promise training-free navigation with interpretable reasoning and less sim-to-real gap. Learned VLN agents such as DUET already benefit from online topological maps with backtracking, but nobody had shown how to express such a map in a form an LLM can reason over. The authors also observe that GPT struggles with precise metric coordinates but handles node IDs and connectivity phrased in language well. Humans, too, keep an updatable work plan rather than logging every thought.
key_idea: Serialize an online-built topological map (node IDs, trajectory, connectivity, and descriptions of unexplored nodes) into the prompt of a single GPT-4/GPT-4V navigation expert, and have it output and iteratively revise an explicit multi-step path plan. This enables global exploration and backtracking in zero-shot VLN.
insight: An LLM uses a map far better when it is given as linguistic topological relations than as metric coordinates. In the GPT-4V ablation on the 72-scene R2R subset, a coordinate map lowered SR from 42.6 to 41.2, while a topological map raised it to 44.9. The best use of the map is free-form multi-step planning rather than DUET-style global action selection over all nodes: global action planning reached only 45.4 SR versus 47.7 for adaptive planning. The map mainly raises the exploration ceiling (GPT-4 OSR goes from 49.5 to 59.7 with the topological map) and enables purposeful backtracking. On REVERIE, 49% of MapGPT episodes backtrack, 80% of which correct an error at least once, versus 18% and 53% for NavGPT. With caption-based GPT-4, the extra exploration costs SPL; GPT-4V avoids this vision-to-text information loss.
method: Single-expert prompt system: one GPT call per step with task description D (background, input definitions, output requirements), raw instruction I, action history H_t, observations O_t of the navigable directions, and action space A_t. The call outputs a thought and one option label. This replaces NavGPT/DiscussNav's multi-expert summarizers (672 input / 115 output tokens per step vs NavGPT's 2,465 / 317).

Two input modes: one-stage GPT-4V takes interleaved images ('Image 0: <Img0> ...'). Two-stage GPT-4/GPT-3.5 takes BLIP-2 captions plus Faster R-CNN object detections per navigable direction, formatted as '<scene>, which also includes <objects>'.
Action space: 'A. stop' plus N options of the form '{label} {direction} Place {id}: {observation}', using six directional phrases (go forward/turn left/turn right/turn around/go up/go down to).

Online topological map: a DUET-style graph G_t of all observed nodes indexed in observation order, updated from simulator-provided neighbors. Nodes are classed as explored, currently accessible, or unexplored-inaccessible.

Map-guided prompt: a 'Trajectory: Place ...' line listing explored node IDs, and a 'Map:' block of 'Place X is connected with Places ...' for each explored node (no GPS coordinates). Accessible nodes are annotated with their IDs in the action space. Unexplored inaccessible nodes are given as 'Supplementary Info' (raw images for GPT-4V, captions for GPT-4) to support backtracking choices.

Adaptive path planning: at each step the LLM receives its previous plan P_{t-1} (initialized to 'Navigation has just started, with no planning yet'). It outputs thought T_t, an updated multi-step plan P_t over multiple candidate nodes or sub-goals (including backtracking), and action a_t.

REVERIE adaptation: small edits to the task description tell the agent to ignore object-interaction verbs and to check the target object in the 'Surroundings' object list before stopping. Object grounding is not performed.

setting.backbone: GPT-4V (frozen, one-stage, image inputs). Also GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 (frozen, two-stage) with BLIP-2 captions + Faster R-CNN detections.
setting.observation: RGB views toward each navigable viewpoint (raw images for GPT-4V; BLIP-2 captions + Faster R-CNN object lists for GPT-4/3.5), plus directional phrases; REVERIE additionally gets a 'Surroundings' object list
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (choose an adjacent navigable viewpoint or stop; backtracking done via planned multi-step moves)
setting.privileged: Standard MP3D nav-graph connectivity. On REVERIE, uses the dataset-provided object list derived from REVERIE bounding-box annotations ('Surroundings') to decide stopping; not used on R2R.

numbers_note: The 72-scene/216-trajectory R2R set is NavGPT's sampled subset. The paper does not name its source split, so it is filed as val-unseen subset by convention. R2R val-unseen results are on '11 scenes and 783 trajectories' as stated; it is unclear whether all 2,349 instructions or one per path were used, and it is recorded as full. Ablation (Table 4, 72 scenes) values for further variants: GPT-4 no map 32.9 SR, GPT-4 topological map without planning 37.5 SR; GPT-4V no map 42.6 SR, coordinate map 41.2, topological map 44.9, topological map + global action planning 45.4. REVERIE HAMT/DUET baselines were re-tested on the same 500-instruction subset.
results: Numbers below are success rate (SR). On NavGPT's 72-scene R2R subset, MapGPT with GPT-4V reaches 47.7 SR / 38.1 SPL, and with GPT-4 41.2 SR. The strongest baseline, DiscussNav (GPT-4, 5 experts, single prediction), gets 37.5 SR / 33.3 SPL, so the gain is about 10 points. On R2R val-unseen, MapGPT with GPT-4V gets 43.7 SR / 34.8 SPL versus NavGPT's 34 SR / 29 SPL. On a 500-instruction REVERIE val-unseen subset it reaches 31.6 SR, versus NavGPT's 19.2 (about 12 points), matching HAMT's 31.6 SR (re-tested) but still below DUET's 45.8. The GPT-4 two-stage variant has high OSR but low SPL because of longer exploration.
limitations: Evaluated only in the discrete Matterport3D simulator with teleportation between nav-graph nodes; no real-world or continuous-environment tests.

Large gap remains to pretrained and fine-tuned agents (e.g., R2R val-unseen: ScaleVLN 81 SR, DUET 72 SR). Evaluation uses subsets (72 scenes; 500 REVERIE instructions) because of API cost, and relies on closed GPT APIs.

The GPT-4 two-stage variant suffers low SPL from over-exploration caused by caption information loss. REVERIE object grounding is ignored, and stopping relies on the dataset's annotated object list. Failure cases include stopping at similar-looking rooms and not backtracking in time.
